Arithmetic Galois representations and conductors

Galois representations and modularity · 3 definitions · 2 constructions

R01.1Continuous representations and integral models

Continuity, descent of the coefficient field, and lattice independence of the residual semisimplificationconstruction

Stage content recorded here (the general statements are NOT proved in the passages read): for a continuous representation rho: G -> GL_n(K_lambda) with G compact and K_lambda a local field, compactness of rho(G) gives a stable lattice, so rho may be conjugated into GL_n(O_lambda); reduction modulo the maximal ideal then gives a residual representation whose SEMISIMPLIFICATION is independent of the chosen lattice, by the Brauer-Nesbitt theorem in characteristic p; a continuous representation into GL_2(F_p-bar) with the discrete topology has finite image and hence descends to a finite coefficient field. What the sources read actually contain: Serre 1987, 1.1, notes that the image of a continuous rho: G_Q -> GL(V), V of dimension 2 over F_p-bar, is a finite group isomorphic to a subgroup of GL_2(F_q) for a suitable power q of p (and that one can take F_q generated by the traces if p != 2 or rho is irreducible); Deligne-Serre 6.12 passes from rho_lambda over K_lambda to the residual representation by 'quitte a remplacer rho_lambda par une representation isomorphe, on peut supposer que rho_lambda(G) est contenu dans GL_2(O-hat_lambda)', reduces mod lambda, takes the semisimplification and descends it to the field generated by the coefficients of its characteristic polynomials (Lemme 6.13).

Hypotheses

  • compactness of the image is what produces the lattice; Deligne-Serre 6.12 asserts the conjugation into GL_2(O-hat_lambda) without argument
  • independence of the lattice holds only after semisimplification; the reduction itself depends on the lattice
  • the descent to a finite field uses that the target is discrete, so continuity forces finite image
  • the Brauer-Nesbitt theorem in characteristic p is used but was NOT read in a source in this pass

ArithmeticGaloisRepresentations:R01.1/continuity-descent-and-lattice-independence

R01.2Decomposition groups, inertia and Weil–Deligne representations

Tame inertia, the level of a character, and the fundamental characters of levels one and twodefinition

Let G_p = Gal(Qbar_p/Q_p), I its inertia subgroup, I_p the wild inertia (the largest pro-p subgroup of I), and I_t = I/I_p the tame quotient, which is identified with the inverse limit of the F_{p^n}^*. A character of I_t is said to be of level n if it factors through F_{p^n}^* and through no F_{p^m}^* for m a proper divisor of n. The two fundamental characters psi, psi' of level 2 are the characters I_t -> F_{p^2}^* -> F_p-bar^* corresponding to the two embeddings of F_{p^2} into F_p-bar; the fundamental character of level 1 is the mod p cyclotomic character chi, and psi psi' = chi. For a 2-dimensional continuous rho_p: G_p -> GL(V) over F_p-bar, I_p acts trivially on the semisimplification V^{ss}, so I_t acts diagonalizably on V^{ss} through two characters phi, phi'; these are of level 1 or of level 2, and in the level-2 case phi' = phi^p and phi = phi'^p. A separate source fixes notation for the lifts: omega_p denotes the Teichmuller lift of the mod p cyclotomic character, and omega_{p,2} a fundamental character of level 2 valued in F_{p^2}^*, with the same symbol used for its Teichmuller lift and for all its l-adic incarnations.

Hypotheses

  • the identification of I_t with the inverse limit of the F_{p^n}^* and the triviality of I_p on a semisimple F_p-bar-representation are both quoted from an external source in the text read
  • 'level' is a property of a character of I_t, not of a representation of G_p
  • the dichotomy level 1 versus level 2 is specific to dimension 2; the argument uses that conjugation by a Frobenius lift acts on I_t by u -> u^p and hence permutes {phi, phi'}
  • the Teichmuller lifts and their l-adic incarnations for arbitrary l are denoted by the same symbols in the second source; the ambiguity is deliberate and must be tracked

ArithmeticGaloisRepresentations:R01.2/tame-inertia-and-fundamental-characters

Grothendieck's monodromy theorem and the passage from a lambda-adic representation to a Weil-Deligne representationconstruction

Let K be a non-archimedean local field with residue field k of cardinality q, l a prime different from the residue characteristic p, E_lambda a finite extension of Q_l, and (V, rho) a lambda-adic representation of W(Kbar/K), i.e. a continuous representation on a finite-dimensional E_lambda-vector space. Grothendieck's theorem (the source's 8.2, whose proof the source refers to [13] = Serre-Tate, Good reduction of abelian varieties): there exists a nilpotent N in End(V)(-1) such that for sigma in a subgroup of FINITE INDEX of the inertia group I one has rho(sigma) = exp(N.t_l(sigma)); this N is unique, hence Galois-invariant, and for w in W(Kbar/K) it satisfies rho(w) N rho(w)^{-1} = q^{v'(w)} N. Here (2.2.2-2.2.4) v' : Gal(Kbar/K) -> Gal(kbar/k) is the reduction map, W(kbar/k) = Z is generated by the arithmetic Frobenius phi: x -> x^q, W(Kbar/K) consists of the sigma with v'(sigma) an integral power of phi, and the geometric Frobenius is F = phi^{-1}; so v'(w) is read as the integer n with v'(w) = phi^n. Consequently rho(Phi) N rho(Phi)^{-1} = q N for an arithmetic Frobenius lift Phi (v'(Phi) = 1) and rho(F) N rho(F)^{-1} = q^{-1} N for a geometric Frobenius F. Definition 8.4.1: for E a field of characteristic 0, a representation of 'W(Kbar/K) over E is a pair (rho', N) of a finite-dimensional representation rho': W(Kbar/K) -> GL(V) over E and a nilpotent endomorphism N of V with (8.4.1.1) rho'(w) N rho'(w)^{-1} = q^{v'(w)} N. Construction 8.4.2 attaches such a pair to a lambda-adic (V, rho) after CHOOSING a geometric Frobenius F in W(Kbar/K) and an isomorphism T: Q_l(1) -> Q_l: rho'(F^n sigma) = rho(F^n sigma) exp(-t_l(sigma) N) for sigma in I, and N' in End(V) corresponds to N via T. Lemme 8.4.3 shows the isomorphism class of (rho', N') depends only on rho and not on the choices of F and T.

Hypotheses

  • lambda must have residue characteristic different from that of K; this is the l different from p hypothesis of the stage
  • the nilpotent N of Theorem 8.2 lies in End(V)(-1), i.e. it is Tate-twisted; the untwisted N' of 8.4.2 depends on the choice of T, and changing T to aT replaces N' by aN'
  • quasi-unipotence is only on a subgroup of FINITE INDEX of inertia; rho itself need not be unipotent on all of I
  • the construction 8.4.2 depends on choosing a GEOMETRIC Frobenius F and a trivialization T of Z_l(1); Lemme 8.4.3 removes the dependence only up to isomorphism
  • the source's proof of Lemme 8.4.3 changes F to F.rho (rho in I), giving an isomorphic pair via conjugation by A = exp((1-q^{-1})^{-1} t_l(rho)), and T to aT, and shows (rho', N') is isomorphic to (rho', aN') for every a (printed 'a in E', meaning a nonzero) by decomposing V into generalized eigenspaces V^alpha of F^n, with N V^alpha contained in V^{q^{-n} alpha}

R01.3Artin and Swan conductors

The Artin conductor exponent, its wild part, and the prime-to-p conductor N(rho-bar)definition

Let l be a prime different from p and choose an extension of the l-adic valuation to Qbar; let G_0 superset G_1 superset ... be the corresponding ramification groups of the finite image G of rho, and V^i the subspace fixed by G_i. Define n(l, rho) = sum over i >= 0 of (1/[G_0 : G_i]) dim(V/V^i). Equivalently n(l, rho) = dim V/V^{G_0} + b(V), where b(V) is the 'wild invariant' of the G_0-module V. Consequences: (a) n(l, rho) is a nonnegative integer; (b) n(l, rho) = 0 if and only if G_0 = 1, i.e. rho is unramified at l; (c) n(l, rho) = dim V/V^{G_0} if and only if G_1 = 1, i.e. rho is tamely ramified at l. The prime-to-p conductor is N = product over l different from p of l^{n(l, rho)}; it is prime to p by construction.

Hypotheses

  • the definition uses the ramification filtration in LOWER numbering of the finite quotient through which rho factors at l, and the sum is over i >= 0 including the wild part
  • integrality of n(l, rho) is a theorem (it is the content of (a)), not evident from the formula
  • the definition is the characteristic-zero one, applied to a residual representation; the source says so explicitly and restricts the product to places prime to p
  • the equivalence n(l, rho) = dim V/V^{G_0} characterises tameness; the wild term b(V) is not omitted at l = 2 or 3

G7Tensor constructions and polarized Galois representations

The 'enormous' condition for Taylor-Wiles data, its failure when p divides n, and its invariance under coefficient extensiondefinition

Let k be an algebraic extension of F_p and ad^0 the space of trace-zero matrices in M_{n x n}(k) with the adjoint GL_n(k)-action. An ABSOLUTELY IRREDUCIBLE subgroup H of GL_n(k) is called enormous over k if: (1) H has no nontrivial quotient of p-power order; (2) H^0(H, ad^0) = H^1(H, ad^0) = 0; (3) for any simple k[H]-submodule W of ad^0 there is a REGULAR SEMISIMPLE h in H with W^h nonzero. The condition depends only on the image of H in PGL_n(k). If p divides n then NO subgroup of GL_n(k) is enormous, because ad^0 then contains the scalar matrices. Lemma 6.2.30: for an algebraic extension k'/k and H contained in GL_n(k), H is enormous over k if and only if it is enormous over k'. The definition is essentially equivalent to the one in the literature cited as [KT17, Def. 4.10] provided k is large enough to contain all eigenvalues of the elements of H.

Hypotheses

  • H must be absolutely irreducible as part of the definition, not merely irreducible
  • condition (3) requires h to be REGULAR SEMISIMPLE; dropping regularity changes the condition
  • the condition is vacuous - unsatisfiable - when p divides n; the source says so explicitly
  • the equivalence with [KT17, Def. 4.10] holds only under the extra hypothesis that k contains all eigenvalues of elements of H
  • in the applications the group is the image of rho restricted to G_{F(zeta_p)}, not the image of rho itself

Arithmetic statistics, counting fields and Selmer distributions

Analytic number theory · 1 definition · 1 construction

ST.0Families, heights and measures

The invariants I and J, the height on binary quartic forms and on elliptic curves, and the eligible pairsdefinition

For f(x,y) = a x^4 + b x^3 y + c x^2 y^2 + d x y^3 + e y^4 the ring of SL_2^{pm}(R)-invariants is generated by I(f) = 12ae - 3bd + c^2 (degree 2) and J(f) = 72ace + 9bcd - 27ad^2 - 27eb^2 - 2c^3 (degree 3), which are relative invariants for GL_2 with I(gamma f) = (det gamma)^4 I(f) and J(gamma f) = (det gamma)^6 J(f); the discriminant is Delta(f) = (4I(f)^3 - J(f)^2)/27 and the height is H(f) := H(I,J) = max{|I|^3, J^2/4}. Every elliptic curve over Q is isomorphic to a unique E_{A,B} : y^2 = x^3 + Ax + B with A, B integers and, for every prime p, p^6 not dividing B whenever p^4 | A; its naive height is H(E_{A,B}) = max{4|A^3|, 27B^2}, and with I(E) = -3A, J(E) = -27B one has H'(E) := max{|I(E)|^3, J(E)^2/4} and 27 H(E) = 4 H'(E), so H and H' induce the same ordering. A pair (I,J) in Z x Z occurs as the invariants of an integral binary quartic form (is ELIGIBLE) if and only if one of: I == 0 (mod 3) and J == 0 (mod 27); I == 1 (mod 9) and J == +-2 (mod 27); I == 4 (mod 9) and J == +-16 (mod 27); I == 7 (mod 9) and J == +-7 (mod 27).

Hypotheses

  • The GL_2 action is by linear substitution gamma . f(x,y) = f((x,y) gamma), a LEFT action (3), for which I and J have weights (det gamma)^4 and (det gamma)^6 (5). From Section 2.4 on, the source instead uses the twisted action (det gamma)^{-2} f((x,y) gamma) ((21), (32)), under which I and J are invariant and PGL_2 acts. [Corrected in review: the draft said only that 'a different convention changes the exponents'.]
  • The minimality condition on the Weierstrass model is exactly 'p^4 | A implies p^6 does not divide B'; without it the model, and hence the height, is not unique
  • The two heights H and H' differ by the factor 27/4; every asymptotic constant depends on which is used, but the induced ordering is the same
  • Theorem 1.7 is an if-and-only-if characterization modulo 27 only; no other congruence conditions are needed

ST.1Parametrizations by orbits

Theorem 2.14 and Proposition 2.16: the auxiliary embedding of binary quartic orbits into pairs of ternary quadratic formsconstruction

There is a map phi from V_Z (integral binary quartic forms) to W_{Z,1} (a slice of the space W_Z of pairs of integral ternary quadratic forms) inducing a canonical bijection between PGL_2(Z)-orbits on V_Z and F_{Z,1} x SO(A_1,Z)-orbits on W_{Z,1}, and hence a natural map psi : PGL_2(Z)\V_Z -> (GL_2(Z) x SL_3(Z))\W_Z. An element of (GL_2(Z) x SL_3(Z))\W_Z with nonzero discriminant has at most 12 preimages under psi. Interpreted via the ring-theoretic dictionaries, (GL_2(Z) x SL_3(Z))\W_Z parametrizes pairs (Q,R) with Q a quartic ring and R a cubic resolvent ring, PGL_2(Z)\V_Z parametrizes triples (Q,R,x) with R monogenic and x a monogenizer, and psi forgets the monogenizer.

Hypotheses

  • The PGL_2 action on V used here is the twisted one gamma . f(x,y) = (det gamma)^{-2} f((x,y) gamma); the PGL_2(Z)-orbits on V_Z coincide with the GL_2(Z)-orbits because -Id acts trivially
  • The bound of 12 preimages requires nonzero discriminant
  • The ring-theoretic interpretations are quoted: (Q,R) from Bhargava's higher composition laws [3], the (Q,R,x) description from Wood [44]

Artin v-stacks, solid and lisse coefficient categories

Geometrisation of local Langlands · 5 definitions · 2 constructions

VS0Artin v-stacks and eligible operations

FS IV.1.1: Artin v-stacks by representable diagonal and a separated cohomologically smooth atlasdefinition

An Artin v-stack is a small v-stack X such that the diagonal Delta_X : X -> X x X is representable in locally spatial diamonds, and such that there exists a surjective map f : U -> X from a locally spatial diamond U that is separated and cohomologically smooth. Separatedness of f forces Delta_X to be quasiseparated. The relative notion over a base S with representable diagonal agrees with the absolute one.

Hypotheses

  • Separatedness of the atlas f is imposed BECAUSE cohomological smoothness has only been defined for separated maps; Fargues-Scholze call this an 'unwanted very mild separatedness condition'
  • Quasiseparatedness of X itself is NOT required and would be far too strong: Bun_G is not quasiseparated, and already [*/G(E)] is not, since G(E) is not quasicompact
  • If one only has an atlas that is surjective as a map of V-STACKS (rather than of pro-etale stacks), then representability of Delta_X in diamonds still has to be proved separately; it may be checked after pullback along a map V -> X x X that is surjective as a map of pro-etale stacks
  • The relative/absolute comparison (Remark IV.1.6) needs Delta_S to be representable in locally spatial diamonds

VStackSheavesAndLisseCategories:VS0/artin-v-stack-definition

FS IV.1.11-IV.1.17: cohomological smoothness for stacky maps and the dualizing complex Rf^! Lambdaconstruction

For f : Y -> X a map of Artin v-stacks admitting a separated, representable, cohomologically smooth surjection g : V -> Y from a locally spatial diamond with f o g separated, f is cohomologically smooth if f o g is, for one equivalently all such g. For such f one defines the invertible dualizing complex Rf^! Lambda in D_et(Y,Lambda) by the compatible system of isomorphisms Rg^!(Rf^! Lambda) = R(f o g)^! Lambda over the category of separated cohomologically smooth g : V -> Y, and sets Rf^! = Rf^! Lambda tensor^L f^*. Rf^! preserves all limits and colimits, hence has a left adjoint Rf_!. f is pure of l-dimension d in (1/2)Z if Rf^! F_l sits in homological degree 2d.

Hypotheses

  • Lambda is killed by an integer n prime to p, or is an adic ring as in ECD Section 26
  • The 'equivalently, one' clause rests on ECD Proposition 23.13 (cohomological smoothness is smooth-local on the source)
  • Convention IV.1.12 makes the existence of g with f o g separated PART of the assertion that f is cohomologically smooth; it is automatic only when X, Y admit perfectoid covers and Delta_X is representable in perfectoid spaces
  • Remark IV.1.14 is an explicit warning: for a compactifiable representable g with dim.trg g < infinity it is NOT clear that Rg^!(Rf^! Lambda) = R(f o g)^! Lambda; this is asserted only for V a locally spatial diamond and g separated cohomologically smooth
  • Fargues-Scholze explicitly do NOT construct Rf_! and Rf^! for general stacky maps; only Rf^! for cohomologically smooth maps of Artin v-stacks
  • The decomposition into pieces pure of l-dimension d may a priori depend on l and involve half-integers

VStackSheavesAndLisseCategories:VS0/shriek-pullback-for-smooth-stacky-maps

VS1ULA, Jacobian criterion and localization

FS IV.2.1: local acyclicity for diamonds requires a constructibility condition in addition to overconvergencedefinition

Let f : X -> S be a compactifiable map of locally spatial diamonds with locally dim.trg f < infinity, and A in D_et(X,Lambda) with n Lambda = 0, n prime to p. A is f-locally acyclic if (a) for all geometric points x of X with image s and every generization t of s, the map RGamma(X_x, A) -> RGamma(X_x x_{S_s} S_t, A) is an isomorphism; and (b) for all separated etale j : U -> X with f o j quasicompact, R(f o j)_!(A|_U) is PERFECT-CONSTRUCTIBLE on S. A is f-universally locally acyclic if this holds after every base change S' -> S along locally spatial diamonds.

Hypotheses

  • Both conditions are required; (b) is automatic in the scheme case under standard finiteness hypotheses but is highly nontrivial for adic spaces. Fargues-Scholze add it because 'in the world of adic spaces, there are not enough specializations to make this an interesting definition' - e.g. there are no specializations from Gr_{G,mu} into Gr_{G,<=mu} minus Gr_{G,mu}
  • X_x = Spa(C(x),C(x)^+) is the STRICT LOCALIZATION, the initial diamond pro-etale over X with a lift of x; the whole-fibre formulation is avoided because actual fibres are only pseudo-adic spaces in Huber's sense
  • The generization set S_t inside S_s is a quasicompact pro-constructible generalizing subspace; condition (a) says A is overconvergent along horizontal lifts of generizations
  • Condition (a) held universally is EQUIVALENT to A being overconvergent (Prop. IV.2.4); so the universal version of (a) alone is a pointwise condition
  • Lambda must be killed by an integer prime to p

VStackSheavesAndLisseCategories:VS1/ula-definition-with-constructibility

FS IV.2.31-IV.2.32: universal local acyclicity for maps of Artin v-stacksdefinition

Let f : X -> S be a map of Artin v-stacks admitting a separated, representable in locally spatial diamonds, cohomologically smooth surjection g : U -> X from a locally spatial diamond with f o g compactifiable of locally finite dim.trg. Then A in D_et(X,Lambda) is f-universally locally acyclic if g^* A is f o g-universally locally acyclic. If f is cohomologically smooth, A is f-universally locally acyclic if and only if p_1^* RHom_Lambda(A,Lambda) tensor^L p_2^* A -> RHom_Lambda(p_1^* A, p_2^* A) is an isomorphism on X x_S X.

Hypotheses

  • The definition requires the existence of a chart g with f o g compactifiable and locally finite dim.trg; well-definedness (independence of g) is exactly Proposition IV.2.13
  • Fargues-Scholze warn that the previous results carry over only 'assuming that the relevant operations are defined in the case of interest - we did not define Rf_! and Rf^! for general stacky maps'
  • Proposition IV.2.32 needs f COHOMOLOGICALLY SMOOTH, which is what permits replacing Rp_2^! by p_2^*

VS2Condensed and solid foundations

Clausen-Scholze solid abelian groups: definition and the structure theoremdefinition

For a profinite set S = lim_i S_i put Z[S]_solid = lim_i Z[S_i], a condensed abelian group receiving S -> Z[S]_solid and hence Z[S] -> Z[S]_solid. A condensed abelian group A is solid if every map S -> A from a profinite set extends uniquely over Z[S]_solid. A complex C in D(Cond(Ab)) is solid if RHom(Z[S]_solid, C) -> RGamma(S,C) = RHom(Z[S],C) is an isomorphism for all profinite S. Theorem 5.8: Solid is an abelian subcategory of Cond(Ab) stable under all limits, colimits and extensions, with compact projective generators the products of copies of Z; the inclusion has a left adjoint M -> M_solid, the unique colimit-preserving extension of Z[S] -> Z[S]_solid; D(Solid) -> D(Cond(Ab)) is fully faithful with image the solid objects, and C is solid if and only if every H^i(C) is solid.

Hypotheses

  • Z[S]_solid is defined only for S PROFINITE, via a chosen presentation as a cofiltered limit; the identification Z[S]_solid = Hom(C(S,Z),Z) shows independence
  • Definition 5.1(ii) (solid object) and 5.1(iii) (solid complex) are a priori different; Scholze explicitly flags that neither implication is clear before Theorem 5.8
  • Remark 5.3 notes that asking the INTERNAL RHom's to agree is a priori stronger, and that this is automatic only by Corollary 6.1(iv)
  • The proof of Theorem 5.8 goes through Lemma 5.9, an abstract criterion requiring an abelian category with colimits and a generating subcategory of compact projectives, plus a vanishing condition on kernels of maps between sums of F-objects

VStackSheavesAndLisseCategories:VS2/solid-abelian-groups

FS VII.1 and VII introduction: solid pro-etale sheaves on a small v-stack and the five-functor formalismconstruction

For X a spatial diamond and quasi-pro-etale j : U -> X written as a cofiltered limit of qcqs etale j_i : U_i -> X, set j_sharp Z-hat = lim_i j_{i!} Z-hat. A pro-etale sheaf F of Z-hat-modules on X is solid if Hom(j_sharp Z-hat, F) -> F(U) is an isomorphism for all such j. This defines a full subcategory D_solid(X,Z_l) of D(X_v, Z_l), compatible with pullback, symmetric monoidal, stable under all limits and colimits, whose inclusion has a left adjoint; solidity of a complex is equivalent to solidity of each cohomology sheaf and may be checked v-locally. For any f : Y -> X, f^* has a right adjoint Rf_* commuting with base change, and also a LEFT adjoint f_sharp ('relative homology') that commutes with base change and satisfies the projection formula. Rf_! does not have its usual properties: for proper finite-dimensional f, Rf_* need not satisfy a projection formula.

Hypotheses

  • Z-hat denotes lim over all nonzero n of Z/nZ; Fargues-Scholze quickly restrict to Z-hat^p = lim over n prime to p
  • The construction of j_sharp Z-hat uses that the pro-system of the U_i is unique; the full subcategory Pro(X_et^{qcqs}) inside X_qproet^{qcqs} is a basis for the quasi-pro-etale topology by ECD Prop. 11.23(ii) and 11.24
  • The resulting formalism is a FIVE-functor formalism: Fargues-Scholze explicitly decline to claim the usual Rf_! behaviour, and note in a footnote that one may treat it as a six-functor formalism in which f^! = f^* for all f
  • D_solid(X,Z_l) is NOT presentable at one fixed universe: it is a large filtered colimit of presentable categories D_solid(X_kappa, Lambda) over uncountable strong limit cardinals kappa
  • A stratification does NOT give a semiorthogonal decomposition on D_solid

VStackSheavesAndLisseCategories:VS2/solid-sheaves-on-v-stacks

VS3Lisse categories and coefficients

FS VII.6.1-VII.6.3: D_lis of an Artin v-stack, its tensor/pullback stability and right adjointdefinition

Fix l != p and a discrete Z_l-algebra Lambda, interpreted as the condensed ring Lambda = Z_l tensor_{Z_l,disc} Lambda_disc. For X an Artin v-stack, D_lis(X,Lambda) inside D_solid(X,Lambda) is the smallest triangulated subcategory stable under all direct sums containing f_sharp Lambda for every f : Y -> X that is separated, representable in locally spatial diamonds, and l-cohomologically smooth. It is stable under the solid tensor product, and f^* maps D_lis(X,Lambda) into D_lis(Y,Lambda) for f a map of Artin v-stacks. The inclusion admits a right adjoint A -> A_lis whose kernel is the class of A with A(Y) = 0 for all such f : Y -> X.

Hypotheses

  • 'lisse' refers to the lisse-etale site of an Artin stack in the sense of Laumon-Moret-Bailly, NOT to local constancy of the objects; Fargues-Scholze say this explicitly
  • A single prime l must be fixed 'for a technical reason'; the coefficients are the condensed ring Z_l tensor_{Z_l,disc} Lambda_disc, not the discrete ring
  • X must be an ARTIN v-stack; for a general small v-stack the definition can be made but 'there might be very few objects'
  • Fargues-Scholze write 'The existence of the right adjoint is formal' and that 'The description of the kernel is formal'. What is NOT formal is the ambient set-up: D_solid(X,Lambda) is not itself presentable but a large filtered colimit of presentable infinity-categories D_solid(X_kappa,Lambda) over uncountable strong limit cardinals kappa, and one must check that D_lis(X,Lambda) is contained in D_solid(X_kappa,Lambda) for some kappa (reduce to X spatial and to quasicompact f, where f_sharp Z_l = lim_m f_sharp Z/l^m Z with each term in D_et(X,Z/l^m Z), then apply [Sch17a, Remark 17.4]) before gluing the right adjoints over all large enough kappa.

Automorphic bundles and classical automorphic forms

Modular and automorphic forms · 1 definition · 2 constructions

B2Automorphic bundles and realizations

The bundle attached to a representation, and the two weight categories that must be distinguishedconstruction

Two categories of weights appear and must be kept distinct. (i) Automorphy factors valued in C^* give automorphic LINE bundles, and these are the classical scalar weights. (ii) Automorphy factors valued in the centralizer Cent_{h_0}(G(C)) of the Hodge cocharacter give automorphic VECTOR bundles W for arbitrary finite-dimensional representations W of that centralizer. The source states explicitly that not all modular forms arise from case (i). Bundles in case (ii) coming from representations of the whole group G(C) carry an integrable connection, and their canonical extensions carry a connection with log poles. The source states only this direction; the drafted 'exactly those' and 'only those' are not in it (reviewer correction). The B2 stage text likewise warns against assigning the flat structure to every automorphic bundle. In the second source the corresponding object is a representation rho of the Levi L_{n,(n)} = GL_1 x Res_{F/Q} GL_n of the maximal parabolic of the quasi-split unitary similitude group, with the attached locally free sheaf E_{U,rho} on the Shimura variety X_{n,U} (U neat), whose global sections over the canonical extension are the holomorphic automorphic forms of weight rho and level U.

Hypotheses

  • the group whose representations give weights is the centralizer of h_0 in G(C), i.e. a Levi, not the whole group
  • the source attaches the integrable connection, and the log connection on the canonical extension, to representations restricted from G(C); it says nothing about other automorphic bundles (reviewer correction of 'is where connections live')
  • in the concrete unitary-similitude setting the weight group is the Levi of a specific maximal parabolic, and the Shimura variety is NOT proper
  • the relation between sections of the analytic bundle and the algebro-geometric one is the content of the comparison the stage requires; it is not read here

AutomorphicBundles:B2/automorphic-vector-bundles-from-representations-of-the-centralizer

B3Canonical and subcanonical extensions

Canonical and subcanonical extensions on a toroidal compactification, and why the minimal one does not workconstruction

For a finite-dimensional representation W of the centralizer of h_0 in G(C) the associated automorphic vector bundle W over Gamma\D in general does NOT extend to a vector bundle over the minimal compactification (Gamma\D)^min; the source notes this is consistent with the boundary of the minimal compactification having high codimension. It does, however, admit CANONICAL EXTENSIONS W^can to vector bundles over the toroidal compactifications (Gamma\D)^tor_Sigma, whose SECTIONS ARE INDEPENDENT OF Sigma. When W is the restriction of a representation of the whole group G(C), the bundle W carries an integrable connection, and W^can carries an integrable connection WITH LOG POLES along the boundary, coinciding with the one of Deligne's canonical extension. The SUBCANONICAL extension is W^sub = W^can(-infinity), where infinity denotes the boundary divisor (Gamma\D)^tor minus (Gamma\D) with its REDUCED structure; its global sections are, in the source's words, '(roughly speaking) useful for studying cusp forms' (reviewer correction of the drafted 'are what is used for cusp forms'; the precise identification with cusp forms is stated in the second source for its setting). The cohomology of W^can and W^sub is the coherent cohomology of the toroidal compactification, and it is this algebro-geometric formulation that permits modular forms in mixed or positive characteristic over integral models. The same construction appears in the unitary-similitude setting of the second source: a locally free E_{U,rho} on X_{n,U} with canonical locally free extension E_{U,Delta,rho} to the smooth compactification X_{n,U,Delta} whose boundary is a simple normal crossings divisor, and E^sub_{U,Delta,rho} = the product of E_{U,Delta,rho} with the ideal sheaf of the boundary, whose global sections are the holomorphic cusp forms of weight rho and level U - again independent of Delta.

Hypotheses

  • the canonical extension is on a TOROIDAL compactification and depends on a choice of admissible fan Sigma (resp. auxiliary data Delta); only the SPACES OF SECTIONS are independent of that choice, not the sheaf
  • the log connection is available only for W restricted from a representation of the whole group G(C), not for an arbitrary representation of the centralizer
  • the subcanonical extension is the twist by the ideal sheaf of the REDUCED boundary divisor; the reducedness is part of the definition
  • in the second source the compactification is required to be SMOOTH with simple normal crossings boundary; the canonical extension is asserted locally free there

AutomorphicBundles:B3/canonical-and-subcanonical-extensions

B4Classical forms and explicit weights

The classical definition of a modular form by an automorphy factor, and the cocycle identity it forcesdefinition

In the source's classical formulation, a holomorphic modular form is a holomorphic f: D -> C satisfying (1) the AUTOMORPHY CONDITION f(gamma Z) = j(gamma, Z) f(Z) for all gamma in Gamma and Z in D, for an automorphy factor j: Gamma x D -> C^* defining the weight of f; and (2) the GROWTH CONDITION that f(Z) stays bounded near D^* minus D, with f a cusp form when in addition f(Z) -> 0 as Z -> D^* minus D. When Gamma is neat, the growth condition implies that the section represented by f extends to a section of a line bundle over the minimal compactification (Gamma\D)^min = Gamma\D^*. The automorphy factor is exactly the datum making f a section of an automorphic line bundle over Gamma\D; the line bundles used in the classical embedding theorem are powers of the canonical bundle, i.e. the top exterior power of the cotangent bundle of Gamma\D. CORRECTION TO THE SOURCE: the source displays the cocycle condition as j(gamma' gamma, Z) = j(gamma', Z) j(gamma, Z). That is inconsistent with its own automorphy condition: applying the automorphy condition twice gives f(gamma' gamma Z) = j(gamma', gamma Z) f(gamma Z) = j(gamma', gamma Z) j(gamma, Z) f(Z), so the correct identity for a LEFT action is j(gamma' gamma, Z) = j(gamma', gamma Z) j(gamma, Z). The reviewer confirmed the printed form on the page image of p. 49 (300 dpi): it reads j(gamma' gamma, Z) = j(gamma', Z) j(gamma, Z), so this is a typo in the source and not an extraction artefact. (The drafted evidence, two text extractions from the same text layer, could not by itself exclude an artefact.) The atlas stage text for B4 states the correct identity.

Hypotheses

  • the growth condition's consequence - extension of the section over the minimal compactification - is stated only when Gamma is NEAT
  • the automorphy factor takes values in C^*, so this formulation captures only LINE bundles; vector-valued weights need automorphy factors valued in the centralizer of h_0 in G(C), which is treated separately
  • the cocycle identity as printed in the source is wrong; the correct left-action identity carries the argument gamma Z in the first factor
  • the atlas stage text further requires deriving the RIGHT-action formula rather than reusing the left-action one; no source read here does that derivation

Berkovich spaces, tropical curves and nonarchimedean arithmetic

p-adic Hodge theory and p-adic geometry · 1 definition

TB.2Semistable models and skeletons of curves

Semistable vertex sets, semistable decompositions and the skeleton of a curvedefinition

Standing conventions of the source (Section 3 opening): K is algebraically closed and complete with respect to a nontrivial nonarchimedean valuation; X is a smooth connected algebraic curve over K, X̂ is its smooth completion (a curve, not an analytification) and D = X̂ ∖ X is the finite set of punctures. Analytifications are written X^an and X̂^an. A semistable vertex set of X̂ is a finite set V of type-2 points such that X̂^an ∖ V is a disjoint union of open balls and finitely many open annuli; a semistable vertex set of X additionally has the punctures in distinct open-ball components. The skeleton Σ(X, V) = V ∪ ⋃ Σ(A) over the generalized open annuli A of the decomposition; the completed skeleton Σ̂(X, V) is its closure in X̂^an, equal to Σ(X, V) ∪ D, a graph with vertex set V ∪ D whose open edges are the skeleta of the annuli. (Lemma 3.2) The limit boundary of an open ball component is a single vertex; an open annulus component S(a)^+ has σ: (0, r) → A (r = val(a)) extending continuously to [0, r] with endpoints in V (possibly equal); a punctured ball has endpoints one vertex and one puncture. (Lemma 3.4) Σ is closed, compact iff X = X̂; its limit boundary is D; the components of X^an ∖ Σ are open balls with one-point limit boundary in Σ; Σ is the set of points with no affinoid neighbourhood isomorphic to B(1) and disjoint from V.

Hypotheses

  • K algebraically closed and complete with respect to a nontrivial nonarchimedean valuation (the paper's standing assumption); type-2 points; annuli are standard generalized open annuli S(a)^+ with modulus val(a).
  • Semistable vertex sets of X̂ correspond bijectively to isomorphism classes of semistable formal models (Theorem 4.11, not read).

Certified computational number theory and arithmetic data

Computational number theory · 1 definition · 1 construction

CN.0Representations and complexity

The RAM machine model and the bit-complexity convention used by all running-time statementsdefinition

A RAM consists of an unbounded sequence of memory cells m[0], m[1], m[2], ..., each holding an arbitrary integer, together with a program: a finite sequence of instructions of three types. ARITHMETIC instructions have the form gamma <- alpha * beta where * is addition, subtraction, multiplication or integer division (floor), and alpha, beta are of the form c, m[a] or m[m[a]] and gamma of the form m[a] or m[m[a]], with c an integer constant and a a non-negative integer constant. BRANCHING instructions have the form IF alpha REL beta GOTO i with REL one of =, !=, <, >, <=, >=. The HALT instruction stops execution. Execution starts at I_0 and follows branches until HALT. Input and output are assumed to be in memory cells at prescribed locations; no input/output instructions are specified. COST AND SIZE CONVENTIONS (printed pp. 54-55): the running time of a program on an input is the number of instructions executed (1 unit each); the size of an input is the number of memory cells used to represent it; and for a polynomial-time algorithm all numbers stored in memory must be at most a' n^{b'} + c' in absolute value (after t instructions, at most a'(n+t)^{b'} + c' for any algorithm). Large integers are represented as vectors of base-B digits with B a constant power of 2 (Section 3.3). [Added in review: the draft omitted the unit-cost rule and the magnitude restriction on which the model's meaning depends.]

Hypotheses

  • Memory cells may hold arbitrary integers, but the source charges one unit per instruction AND restricts the magnitude of stored numbers polynomially in the input size and running time. It notes that without this restriction some problems could be solved with polynomially many operations on huge numbers that cannot otherwise be solved in polynomial time (reference to Section 3.6). Large integers are digit vectors in a constant base B, so costs quoted in terms of len(n) are RAM step counts under this convention. [Corrected in review: the draft said the unit-cost reading is 'unrealistic' and that the len(n) convention is what gives the statements meaning; the source's model is unit-cost with a magnitude restriction.]
  • The instruction set is finite and fixed; in particular integer division is a primitive, which matters for the division-with-remainder analysis
  • The model is idealized: the source states explicitly that high-level algorithm descriptions 'can be routinely translated into the machine-language of an actual computer' and that the formal model exists 'so that our theorems on the running times of algorithms have a precise mathematical meaning'

ComputationalNumberTheory:CN.0/ram-machine-model-and-bit-complexity

CN.1Primality and factorization

Square-free decomposition, distinct-degree and equal-degree factorization, with operation countsconstruction

Let F be a finite field of characteristic p with q elements and f in F[X] monic of degree l > 0. (Theorem 20.3) If gcd(f, D(f)) = f then f = g(X^p) for some g, and writing g = sum_i a_i X^i one has f = h^p with h = sum_i a_i^{p^{w-1}} X^i. (Theorem 20.4) If f = f_1^{e_1} ... f_r^{e_r} is the factorization into irreducibles then f/gcd(f, D(f)) = prod over those i with e_i not == 0 (mod p) of f_i. (Theorem 20.5) Algorithm SFD computes a square-free decomposition using O(l^2 + l (w-1) len(p)/p) operations in F. (Theorem 20.6) Distinct-degree factorization uses O(l^3 len(q)) operations in F. (Theorems 20.7, 20.8) Equal-degree splitting uses an expected O(k l^2 len(q)) operations in F, for p = 2 and for p > 2 respectively. (Theorem 20.9) The whole Cantor-Zassenhaus algorithm uses an expected O(l^3 len(q)) operations in F, and this bound is tight (attained when the input is irreducible). (Theorem 20.10) Berlekamp's Algorithm B1 uses O(l^3 + l^2 len(q)) operations in F.

Hypotheses

  • All counts are in OPERATIONS IN F, not bit operations; converting requires multiplying by the cost of an F-operation, which is where the RAM/bit model of CN.0 enters
  • q = p^w; the square-free decomposition cost has a term depending on w and p separately because of the p-th power extraction in Theorem 20.3
  • Equal-degree splitting is PROBABILISTIC: the bounds in Theorems 20.7 and 20.8 are expected values, and the failure probability per pair of irreducible factors is 1/2 for p = 2 and at most 5/9 for p > 2
  • Cantor-Zassenhaus as analysed assumes a square-free input; SFD is used as preprocessing and the bound of Theorem 20.9 survives that preprocessing
  • Berlekamp's Algorithm B1 (Theorem 20.10) only computes a basis of the Berlekamp subalgebra B = {alpha : alpha^q = alpha} of F[X]/(f), by Gaussian elimination on an l x l matrix over F; it does not factor f. Stage 2 of Berlekamp's algorithm, which splits f using that basis, is a PROBABILISTIC procedure (success probability at least 1/2 for p = 2 and 4/9 for p > 2 per split, printed pp. 540-541). [Corrected in review: the draft presented B1 as the deterministic factoring alternative.]
  • PLACEMENT NOTE (added in review): the atlas description of FiniteFieldsAndCharacterSums:FF.3 is 'Prove finite-field polynomial factorization, Hensel interfaces and certified point-counting algorithms', and CN.1 requires FF.3. The mathematics of this node, Shoup Chapter 20, is therefore FF.3's declared scope, while CN.1's role is to implement factorization 'using checked factors and irreducibility proofs'. The EXT-08 FiniteFieldsAndCharacterSums packet records Chapter 20 as unread under FF.3. The orchestrator should decide whether to move this node under FF.3 and keep a CN.1 consumer node, or leave it here with an FF.3 -> CN.1 edge.

Classical Serre Modularity

Galois representations and modularity · 2 definitions

R27.1Good-dihedral representations and auxiliary primes

Definition 2.1: good dihedral primedefinition

Let Q: N -> N be defined by Q(1) = 1 and, for n >= 2, Q(n) = the largest prime dividing n. For rho-bar: G_Q -> GL_2(F_p-bar) continuous, a prime q different from p is a good dihedral prime for rho-bar if (i) rho-bar restricted to I_q is of the form diag(psi, psi^q) with psi a NON-TRIVIAL character of I_q whose order is a power of an odd prime t such that t divides q+1 and t > max(Q(N(rho-bar)/q^2), 5, p); and (ii) q is 1 mod 8, and 1 mod r for every prime r with r <= max(Q(N(rho-bar)/q^2), p). If such a q exists, rho-bar is called locally good-dihedral (for the prime q), or q-dihedral.

Hypotheses

  • psi must be nontrivial and of order a power of an ODD prime t with t | q+1 - so psi is of level 2 at q and t does not divide q-1
  • the bound on t is taken against Q(N(rho-bar)/q^2), i.e. the largest prime dividing the prime-to-q part of the conductor, together with 5 and p
  • condition (ii) (q = 1 mod 8 and q = 1 mod r for the primes r in range) is used in the proof of Lemma 6.3(i) to show that q splits or ramifies in any quadratic field K unramified outside the primes at which rho-bar ramifies, both of which are then excluded
  • the definition is a property of the pair (rho-bar, q), and both conditions refer to N(rho-bar), so it is not stable under arbitrary changes of level

ClassicalSerreModularity:R27.1/good-dihedral-prime-definition

R27.2The induction hypotheses and weight reduction

The three families of hypotheses (L_r), (W_r) and (D_r)definition

For an integer r >= 1: (L_r) all rho-bar of S-type are modular provided (a) rho-bar is locally good-dihedral, (b) k(rho-bar) = 2 IF p = 2, and (c) N(rho-bar) is odd and divisible by at most r primes. (W_r) the same with (b) strengthened to k(rho-bar) = 2 for every p. For an integer r >= 0: (D_r) all rho-bar of S-type are modular provided (a) rho-bar is locally good-dihedral, (b) the residue characteristic of rho-bar is an odd prime, and (c) N(rho-bar) is NOT divisible by 2^{r+1}. Obviously (L_r) implies (W_r). Note that (L_r) and (W_r) require the conductor to be odd, while (D_r) allows even conductor with bounded 2-valuation and instead forbids p = 2.

Hypotheses

  • all three hypotheses are restricted to locally good-dihedral rho-bar; this is the device that avoids residually degenerate modularity lifting beyond what Theorem 1.1 already uses
  • (L_r) imposes weight 2 only at p = 2; (W_r) imposes it at all p
  • (D_r) bounds v_2(N(rho-bar)) by r, and excludes p = 2 entirely

CP.0Geometric fibres and period-ring comparison maps

Specializations of A_inf used by the integral comparisondefinition

For a perfectoid field K with ring of integers O, residue field k and tilt O♭ ⊂ K♭, put A_inf = W(O♭) and fix x ∈ A_inf, the Teichmüller lift of a nonzero noninvertible element of O♭ (x is a non-zero-divisor and x ↦ 0 in W(k)). The specialization maps used by the torsion and lattice statements are: (a) Witt reduction A_inf → W(k), which factors as A_inf → W̃ := colim_n A_inf/(x^{1/p^n}) → W(k), the second map being the p-adic completion of the p-torsion-free ring W̃; its kernel Q := ker(W̃ → W(k)) is an A_inf[1/p]-module. (b) The generic-tilt specialization A_inf → W(K♭), which is flat: A_inf,(p) is a discrete valuation ring (valuation = index of the first nonzero Teichmüller coefficient) and W(K♭) is its p-adic completion. (c) θ: A_inf → O, whose kernel is generated by ξ = 1 + [ε^{1/p}] + ... + [ε^{1/p}]^{p−1} when O contains a compatible system ζ_{p^r} (r ≥ 1) of p-power roots of unity with ζ_p primitive in the sense 1 + ζ_p + ... + ζ_p^{p−1} = 0, where ε := (1, ζ_p, ζ_{p^2}, ...) ∈ O♭; put μ := [ε] − 1 and ξ̃ := φ(ξ). Then θ(ξ) = θ(μ) = 0, and when K has characteristic 0 and contains all p-power roots of unity (§3.3) ξ = μ/φ^{−1}(μ), ξ_r = μ/φ^{−r}(μ) and ξ̃_r = φ^r(μ)/μ generate ker θ, ker θ_r and ker θ̃_r. (d) The crystalline maps A_inf → A_crys → B_crys^+ = A_crys[1/p] → B_dR^+ → B_dR, where (Definition 3.22, §3.3 setting) A_crys is the p-adic completion of the A_inf-subalgebra of A_inf[1/p] generated by all ξ^m/m!, B_crys := A_crys[1/μ] = B_crys^+[1/μ] (a Q_p-algebra because μ^{p−1} ≡ ξ^p mod p, so μ^{p−1} ∈ pA_crys), B_dR^+ is the ξ-adic completion of B_crys^+ (a complete discrete valuation ring with residue field K) and B_dR = B_dR^+[1/ξ]; in particular μ is invertible in B_crys by definition, so A_inf → B_crys factors through A_inf[1/μ]. The canonical map from A_inf[1/p] to its μ-adic completion factors through B_crys^+. (e) μ-inversion A_inf → A_inf[1/μ]; for K = C the specialization to W(C♭) factors through A_inf[1/μ] — presupposed, not proved, by the statement of Lemma 4.26 and used through Corollary 4.15 in Theorem 14.5(ii).

Hypotheses

  • K perfectoid field; O = O_K; O♭ its tilt; k its residue field.
  • x ∈ A_inf is the Teichmüller lift of a nonzero noninvertible element of O♭ (§4.2 convention).
  • For (c): O contains a compatible system of p-power roots of unity with ζ_p primitive (Example 3.16, which also allows characteristic p with all ζ_{p^r} = 1). For the statements involving μ in (c)–(e): K has characteristic 0 and contains all p-power roots of unity (standing assumption of §3.3, restated before Lemma 4.18; in §14, K = C is algebraically closed).

Commutative algebra for deformation theory and patching

Commutative algebra · 3 definitions · 2 constructions

R03.1Complete local coefficient categories

The Artinian coefficient category C_Λ, small extensions and fibre productsdefinition

Let Λ be a Noetherian ring and Λ → k a finite ring map to a field (classical case: Λ a complete Noetherian local ring such as a complete DVR O, k its residue field). C_Λ has objects pairs (A, φ) with A an Artinian local Λ-algebra and φ: A/m_A ≅ k a Λ-algebra isomorphism, and morphisms local Λ-algebra maps compatible with φ. A small extension is a surjection B → A whose kernel is a nonzero principal ideal annihilated by m_B; every surjection in C_Λ factors as a composition of small extensions. A map A → B in C_Λ is surjective iff m_A/m_A² → m_B/m_B² is, iff the map of relative cotangent spaces m_A/(m_Λ A + m_A²) → m_B/(m_Λ B + m_B²) is. A fibre product A₁ ×_A A₂ lies in C_Λ if one of the maps is surjective or k/k′ is separable (k′ = Λ/m_Λ), and if A₂ → A is a small extension so is A₁ ×_A A₂ → A₁; without these hypotheses the fibre product can fail to have residue field k. A surjection B → A is essential (any C → B with C → A surjective is itself surjective) iff B/(m_Λ B + m_B²) → A/(m_Λ A + m_A²) is an essential surjection; a further cotangent-space criterion under separability of k/k′ is Lemma 90.3.12, not read here.

Hypotheses

  • Λ Noetherian, Λ → k finite with k a field; then m_Λ is maximal and k/k′ is finite.
  • Fibre products are only asserted in C_Λ under surjectivity of one map or separability of k/k′ (Example 90.3.7 gives a counterexample with k/k′ inseparable).

DeformationAndDerivedPatchingAlgebra:R03.1/artinian-coefficient-category-and-small-extensions

The complete Noetherian local category Ĉ_Λ: limits, completed pushouts and cotangent finitenessconstruction

Ĉ_Λ has objects Noetherian complete local Λ-algebras R with an identification R/m_R ≅ k and local Λ-algebra maps; C_Λ ⊂ Ĉ_Λ is the full subcategory of Artinian objects and every R equals lim_n R/m_R^n with Artinian terms. A map in Ĉ_Λ is surjective iff it is surjective on m/m² (or on relative cotangent spaces). Ĉ_Λ has pushouts, given by the m-adic completion of S₁ ⊗_R S₂ (a Noetherian complete local ring with residue field k), and coproducts of pairs via the completion of R ⊗_Λ S. For S in Ĉ_Λ, dim_k Der_Λ(S, k) < ∞; if Der_Λ(S, k) → Der_Λ(R, k) is injective then R → S is surjective. An inverse system … → A₃ → A₂ → A₁ of surjections in C_Λ with bounded dim_k(m_{A_n}/m²_{A_n}) has limit S in Ĉ_Λ, and the kernels of S → A_n define the m_S-adic topology; its proof uses the auxiliary Lemma 90.4.7: a decreasing sequence of ideals J_n ⊃ m^n with intersection J defines the adic topology on R/J.

Hypotheses

  • Λ Noetherian, Λ → k finite; completed tensor products are taken in Ĉ_Λ, i.e. over an object R of Ĉ_Λ or over Λ with the kernel of the multiplication map to k.
  • An initial object of Ĉ_Λ exists in the classical case (Λ itself) and when k/k′ is separable, but not when k/k′ is inseparable.

R03.2Representability and obstruction algebra

Schlessinger's conditions (S1), (S2) and tangent spacesdefinition

For a category F cofibred in groupoids over C_Λ (in particular a functor F: C_Λ → Sets), (S1) requires that for A₁ → A and a surjection A₂ → A every compatible pair of objects over A₁, A₂ comes from an object over A₁ ×_A A₂ (for functors: F(A₁ ×_A A₂) → F(A₁) ×_{F(A)} F(A₂) surjective, Schlessinger's (H1)); it suffices to check small extensions. (S2) requires the same for A → k and k[ε] → k and, moreover, that two such completions y, y′ over A ×_k k[ε] with maps a: y → x, a′: y′ → x admit b: y → y′ with a = a′ ∘ b (for functors: bijectivity, Schlessinger's (H2)); (S2) then holds with k[ε] replaced by k[V] for any finite-dimensional V. The tangent space is T F = F(k[ε]) (isomorphism classes for predeformation categories); under (S2) (for the functor of isomorphism classes) it is a k-vector space with F(k[V]) = T F ⊗_k V. For a prorepresentable F = Hom(S, −), T F = Der_Λ(S, k), finite-dimensional, and in the classical case equal to the dual of the relative cotangent space.

Hypotheses

  • F cofibred in groupoids over C_Λ; a predeformation category has F(k) equivalent to a point.
  • (S2) passes to the functor of isomorphism classes provided one of the sufficient conditions of Lemma 90.10.5(2) holds: F a predeformation category, F(k) a set or setoid, or Aut_{k[ε]}(x_ε) → Aut_k(x₀) surjective for all x_ε → x₀ over k[ε] → k.

P7Perfect complexes and derived coefficient change

Perfect complexes, Tor-amplitude and minimal complexes over local ringsdefinition

An object K of D(R) is perfect if it is quasi-isomorphic to a bounded complex of finite projective R-modules; equivalently K is pseudo-coherent of finite Tor dimension, and if K has Tor-amplitude in [a, b] it is represented by finite projectives in degrees [a, b]. Perfect objects satisfy two-out-of-three in triangles and are closed under summands; a bounded complex with perfect cohomology is perfect. Projective amplitude in [a, b] means quasi-isomorphism to projectives in degrees [a, b]. Over a local ring (R, m, κ), a pseudo-coherent K is represented by a complex with terms R^{d_i}, d_i = dim_κ H^i(K ⊗^L κ), unique up to isomorphism (minimal complex); two bounded finite projective representatives of the same perfect object become isomorphic after adding trivial complexes locally. Consequently for perfect K over a local ring, K ⊗^L κ = 0 implies K = 0, and the ranks of a minimal complex are determined by K ⊗^L κ. Three amplitudes must be distinguished: the degrees of a chosen complex, the Tor-amplitude, and the degrees of nonzero cohomology.

Hypotheses

  • R commutative; for minimal complexes R local and K pseudo-coherent.
  • Derived completeness hypotheses are needed for Nakayama-type statements for non-pseudo-coherent complexes (supplied by DerivedDeRhamCohomology DD.1, Stacks 15.92.19–15.92.20).

R31.1Towers and completed cohomology

The completed cohomology of the modular tower and the shape of the local-global conjecturedefinition

Conjecture 1.1.1 of the source: if V is an odd irreducible continuous two-dimensional representation of G_Q over a finite extension E of Q_p, unramified outside a finite set of primes, then the GL_2(A_f)-representation Hom_{E[G_Q]}(V, H-hat^1_E) decomposes as a restricted tensor product B(V|G_{Q_p}) tensor (restricted tensor product over l different from p of pi_l(V)). Completed cohomology, homology and arithmetic towers — Part II

Modular and automorphic forms · 1 definition · 2 constructions

CC.0Finite-level towers and support data

The axioms on the tower, and the two standing hypotheses without which nothing is controlleddefinition

Let G_0 be a profinite group with a countable basis of neighbourhoods of the identity consisting of normal open subgroups ... contained in G_r contained in ... contained in G_1 contained in G_0. Suppose given a tower of topological spaces ... -> X_r -> ... -> X_1 -> X_0, each with an action of G_0, such that (1) the maps X_{r+1} -> X_r are G_0-equivariant, and (2) G_r acts trivially on X_r and realizes X_r as a G_0/G_r-torsor over X_0 - in particular all the maps in the tower are FINITE COVERINGS. Two standing hypotheses are imposed from that point on: (a) each X_r is a manifold homotopic to a finite simplicial complex, which is what makes all four families of (co)homology groups finitely generated over the indicated coefficient ring and relates them by the appropriate duality; and (b) G_0 is a p-ADIC ANALYTIC group - the source says that without this 'it seems impossible to control the inverse limits involved in our constructions', and with it Lazard's theorem that Z_p[[G_0]] is noetherian plus Schneider-Teitelbaum's Banach-representation theory bring the limits under control. In the arithmetic application X_r = G(Q)\G(A)/A_infinity^o K_infinity^o G_r K^{infinity,p}, and the resulting modules carry not only the G_0-action but actions of the whole p-adic group G(Q_p), of a completed Hecke algebra T built from spherical Hecke operators at primes l different from p where G and the tame level K^{infinity,p} are unramified, and of the component group pi_0 = (A_infinity K_infinity)/(A_infinity^o K_infinity^o).

Hypotheses

  • the tower must consist of FINITE coverings with G_r acting trivially on X_r and realizing X_r as a G_0/G_r-torsor over X_0; the source imposes this as an axiom and does not say what fails without it (the drafted claim that the Hochschild-Serre spectral sequences of Theorem 1.1(4) would not exist is not in the source; removed by the reviewer)
  • each X_r homotopic to a FINITE simplicial complex: this is what gives finite generation at each level
  • G_0 p-adic analytic: the source states this is essential for controlling the inverse limits, via Lazard's noetherianity of Z_p[[G_0]]
  • the extension of the G_0-action to all of G(Q_p) in the arithmetic setting is asserted by 'the usual argument about limits of (co)homology of arithmetic quotients in the adelic setting' and is not proved in the source

CC.2Completion, derived inverse limits and topology

The four completed (co)homology modules, and the exact sequence separating the completion from the Tate moduleconstruction

Having fixed p, define completed homology and cohomology by H-tilde_bullet = inverse limit over r of H_bullet(X_r, Z_p) and H-tilde^bullet = inverse limit over s of the direct limit over r of H^bullet(X_r, Z/p^s Z), with Borel-Moore and compactly supported variants H-tilde^BM_bullet = inverse limit over r of H^BM_bullet(X_r, Z_p) and H-tilde_c^bullet = inverse limit over s of the direct limit over r of H_c^bullet(X_r, Z/p^s Z). There are natural maps H-tilde_bullet -> H-tilde^BM_bullet and H-tilde_c^bullet -> H-tilde^bullet. Define also H-hat^bullet = the p-adic completion of the direct limit over r of H^bullet(X_r, Z_p), and T_p H^bullet = the p-adic Tate module of that direct limit. Then there is an exact sequence 0 -> H-hat^bullet -> H-tilde^bullet -> T_p H^{bullet+1} -> 0 (1.1), stated in the source without proof. The p-adic completion kills the p-divisible part of the direct limit, while the Tate module sees only the torsion subgroup of that divisible part. Since T_p H^{bullet+1} is p-torsion free and p-adically complete, dualizing gives 0 -> Hom(T_p H^{bullet+1}, Z_p) -> Hom(H-tilde^bullet, Z_p) -> Hom(H-hat^bullet, Z_p) -> 0. The source then quotes Theorem 1.1(3) to identify the middle term with the p-torsion-free quotient of H-tilde_bullet; that consequence is recorded in the duality node (CC.3), because the atlas places Theorem 1.1(3) after CC.2. Remark 1.15: if the Z_p-cohomology of every X_r is p-torsion-free, or more generally of bounded exponent, the Tate-module term vanishes and H-hat^bullet -> H-tilde^bullet is an isomorphism.

Hypotheses

  • the order of the limits is not interchangeable: H-tilde^bullet is inverse limit over s of direct limit over r, and the two other objects H-hat and T_p H are obtained from the SAME direct limit by completion and by Tate module respectively
  • the source states (1.1) without proof. Reviewer derivation: take the colimit over r of the finite-level universal-coefficient sequences 0 -> H^bullet(X_r, Z_p)/p^s -> H^bullet(X_r, Z/p^s Z) -> H^{bullet+1}(X_r, Z_p)[p^s] -> 0 (filtered colimits are exact), then the inverse limit over s; the lim^1 of the left-hand system vanishes because its transition maps are surjective. That lim^1 vanishing is where the stage's warning against formally commuting completion and cohomology is met
  • the dual sequence uses that T_p H^{bullet+1} is p-torsion free AND p-adically complete

CC.7Compact-support and boundary triangles

The Borel-Serre boundary tower and its long exact sequencesconstruction

Each X_r embeds as an open subset of its Borel-Serre compactification X-bar_r; write dX_r = X-bar_r minus X_r for the boundary. As r varies the X-bar_r form a tower to which the completed (co)homology machinery applies, so one may define completed (co)homology spaces H-tilde_bullet(boundary) and H-tilde^bullet(boundary), and there are long exact sequences (1.2) ... -> H-tilde_bullet(boundary) -> H-tilde_bullet -> H-tilde^BM_bullet -> H-tilde_{bullet-1}(boundary) -> ... and (1.3) ... -> H-tilde^{bullet-1}(boundary) -> H-tilde_c^bullet -> H-tilde^bullet -> H-tilde^bullet(boundary) -> ..., stated without proof. (Reviewer: the drafted '(d)' for the boundary is corrected to the source's boundary symbol; the source also describes the stratification of the boundary by proper parabolics P, a Mayer-Vietoris spectral sequence, and the induction formula (1.4) after a colimit over tame levels, at least for p odd - read, not decomposed.) Scholze's Corollary 4.2.2, for the compactly supported completed cohomology of a Shimura variety of Hodge type with tame level K^p contained in the level-N subgroup for some N >= 3 prime to p: the group H-tilde^i_{c, K^p}(Z/p^n Z) (and a fortiori with Z_p coefficients) VANISHES for i > d, where d = dim_C X_K. Corollary 4.2.3: for i > d one has H-tilde^{BM}_i = 0 and H-tilde^{BM}_d is p-torsion free; for i < d the codimension of H-tilde_i over the Iwasawa algebra is at least d - i. If the X_K are compact this gives all of the Calegari-Emerton Conjecture 1.5 in that case, except with non-strict instead of strict inequalities on the codimensions (Scholze prints 'here l_0 = d and q_0 = 0'). Reviewer correction: those values are swapped. With the survey's definitions l_0 = rank G_infinity - rank A_infinity K_infinity and q_0 = (d_R - l_0)/2, where d_R is the real dimension of X_r, only l_0 = 0 and q_0 = d (Scholze's d = dim_C) makes Corollary 4.2.3 match Conjecture 1.5 parts (1), (5) and (7); with l_0 = d and q_0 = 0, part (7) would say H-tilde_n = 0 for all n > 0. For G = Sp_2g the definitions give l_0 = 0 and q_0 = g(g+1)/2 = d directly. Scholze also points to the survey's Theorem 1.4 for the remaining part (2).

Hypotheses

  • the boundary construction needs the Borel-Serre compactification of each X_r and the compatibility of the compactifications along the tower
  • Scholze's results are for Shimura varieties of HODGE type, with a fixed embedding into a Siegel datum, and with the tame level convention K^p contained in the level-N subgroup of G'(A_f^p) for some N >= 3 prime to p
  • Corollary 4.2.3's comparison with Conjecture 1.5 holds with NON-STRICT inequalities and only when the X_K are compact
  • the proof of Corollary 4.2.2 is a statement about the cohomological dimension of a spectral space, and passes through the perfectoid/adic space at infinite level; it is not an argument about the archimedean tower
  • Placement note (reviewer): Corollaries 4.2.2 and 4.2.3 are vanishing and codimension theorems for Hodge-type Shimura varieties deduced from Theorem 4.2.1, which is recorded in the CC.8 node. The CC.7 stage text says such arithmetic vanishing is not a property of the abstract limit functor, the CC.8 text says vanishing remains a TC/IHG/IG/R31 theorem, and the atlas order CC.7 -> CC.8 rules out a link from Theorem 4.2.1 to this node. The corollaries are kept here verbatim pending the orchestrator's decision and are not CC.7 outputs
  • Corollary 4.2.3 also consumes Theorem 1.1(3) in its torsion-corrected form (duality node), the Poincaré duality spectral sequence E_2^{i,j} = E^i(H-tilde_j) => H-tilde^BM_{d_R-i-j} of the survey's 1.3 (stated there without proof, construction deferred to [6], not decomposed in any node) and Venjakob's codimension theory ([63] in Scholze, [18] in the survey; not read)

Crystalline cohomology, de Rham–Witt and logarithmic foundations

p-adic Hodge theory and p-adic geometry · 2 definitions · 3 constructions

CR.4Ordinary and relative de Rham–Witt complexes

Dieudonné complexesdefinition

A Dieudonné complex is a cochain complex of abelian groups (M*,d) with a map of graded abelian groups F:M*→M* satisfying dF(x)=pF(dx); morphisms commute with d and F. For a p-torsion-free complex, (η_p M)^n={x∈p^nM^n : dx∈p^{n+1}M^{n+1}} is a subcomplex of M*[p^{-1}] (Construction 2.1.3; for complexes in nonnegative degrees η_pM⊆M, footnote 1). For termwise p-torsion-free M, a Dieudonné structure F is equivalent to a map of cochain complexes α_F:M*→(η_pM)*, α_F(x)=p^nF(x) for x∈M^n, with inverse F(x)=p^{-n}α(x).

Hypotheses

  • p is a prime, fixed throughout the source (BLM lines 237 and 463: 'a prime p which is implicitly fixed throughout the sequel').
  • Termwise p-torsion-freeness is required for the equivalence with the décalage description, not for the definition of a Dieudonné complex.

CrystallineCohomology:CR.4/dieudonne-complex

Saturated Frobeniusdefinition

A Dieudonné complex is saturated when it is termwise p-torsion-free and F:M^n→{x∈M^n:dx∈pM^{n+1}} is bijective in every degree. Equivalently, α_F:M→η_p M is an isomorphism.

Hypotheses

  • A Dieudonné complex; saturation includes p-torsion-freeness.

CrystallineCohomology:CR.4/saturated-frobenius

Verschiebung and the differentialconstruction

On a saturated Dieudonné complex define V uniquely by F(Vx)=px. It is injective and satisfies FV=VF=p, FdV=d and Vd=p dV.

Hypotheses

  • The complex is saturated; in particular F is injective and M is p-torsion-free.

CrystallineCohomology:CR.4/verschiebung-identities

Saturation by iterated décalageconstruction

Every Dieudonné complex M* admits a saturation M*→Sat(M*): a map to a saturated complex through which every map to a saturated complex factors uniquely. First quotient by the graded subgroup T* of elements killed by a power of p; on the p-torsion-free quotient take the direct limit of the sequence M*→(η_pM)*→(η_pη_pM)*→⋯ whose transition maps are α_F, η_p(α_F), η_p(η_p(α_F)),… (display (8)). Saturation is left adjoint to the inclusion DC_sat↪DC.

Hypotheses

  • A Dieudonné complex; no initial saturation or p-torsion-freeness assumption.

CrystallineCohomology:CR.4/saturation-colimit

The de Rham–Witt completion towerconstruction

For saturated M* form W_r(M)*=M*/(im V^r+im dV^r) for r≥0 (W_0(M)*=0), the restriction maps Res:W_{r+1}(M)*→W_r(M)*, and the completion W(M)*=lim_r W_r(M)*. F descends to F:W_r(M)*→W_{r−1}(M)* and V to V:W_r(M)*→W_{r+1}(M)*; passing to the limit makes W(M)* a Dieudonné complex, the construction is functorial, and the tautological map ρ_M:M*→W(M)* is a map of Dieudonné complexes (Remark 2.5.3).

Hypotheses

  • M is saturated; r≥0 and W_0(M)=0.

Étale cohomology · 2 definitions

DWP.2Purity for symplectic local systems

Setting of Weil I §3: lisse Q_ℓ-sheaves on an open U_0 ⊆ P^1 over F_q, the local factors det(1 − F_x t, F_0), the L-function Z(U_0, F_0, t), the log-derivative identity (1.5.3) and Grothendieck's trace formula (1.14.3)definition

(3.1): U_0 is a curve over F_q, complement in P^1 of a finite set of closed points; U its base change to F̄_q; u a closed point; F_0 a lisse ('constant tordu') Q_ℓ-sheaf on U_0 with pullback F to U. For β ∈ Z, F_0 is of weight β if for every x ∈ |U_0| the eigenvalues of F_x on F_0,x̄ (1.13: F_x = F^{deg x}, well defined up to isomorphism) are algebraic numbers all of whose complex conjugates have absolute value q_x^{β/2}; e.g. Q_ℓ(r) has weight −2r. (1.14): Z(U_0, F_0, t) = ∏_{x ∈ |U_0|} det(1 − F_x t^{deg x}, F_0)^{-1} ∈ Q_ℓ[[t]]; by (1.5.3) — for an endomorphism F of a vector space V, t d/dt log det(1 − F t, V)^{-1} = Σ_{n>0} Tr(F^n, V) t^n — its logarithmic derivative is Σ_n Σ_{x ∈ X_0(F_{q^n})} Tr(F_x^n, F_0) t^n (1.14.2), and the Lefschetz trace formula (1.12.1) gives (1.14.3): Z(U_0, F_0, t) = ∏_i det(1 − F^* t, H^i_c(U, F))^{(−1)^{i+1}}, an identity in Q_ℓ[[t]].

Hypotheses

  • F_0 lisse (locally constant, 'constant tordu') Q_ℓ-sheaf; U_0 ⊆ P^1 open over F_q; the trace formula (1.12.1) is quoted from SGA 5 (Deligne's (2.14 D): the proof is 'hélas' in SGA 5)
  • Weights are defined via absolute values of all complex conjugates of algebraic eigenvalues

DWP.7The fundamental direct-image theorem and sharp cohomological bounds

Weil II §1.2: pure numbers, punctually pure and mixed sheaves, stabilities, and ι-weightsdefinition

(1.2.1): for q a prime power and n ∈ Z, α is pure of weight n rel. q if it is algebraic and all its complex conjugates have absolute value q^{n/2}; 'number' means element of Q̄_ℓ. (1.2.2): for X of finite type over Z and F a Q̄_ℓ-sheaf on X, F is punctually pure (of weight n) if for every closed x the eigenvalues of F_x are pure of weight n rel. N(x); F is mixed if it has a finite filtration with punctually pure successive quotients, whose weights (of the nonzero quotients) are the punctual weights of F. The zero sheaf is pure of every weight and mixed with empty weight set. Variants (1.2.3)-(1.2.4): representations of Gal(k̄/k) for finite k, Weil sheaves, and Frobenius-modules. Stabilities (1.2.5): punctually pure sheaves of weight n are stable under quotients, subsheaves, extensions, inverse images and direct images by finite morphisms; tensor products add weights and the dual of a lisse punctually pure sheaf of weight n has weight −n; mixed sheaves are stable under the same operations and tensor products; Q̄_ℓ(1) is punctually pure of weight −2. (1.2.6): for an isomorphism ι: Q̄_ℓ ≅ C, w_q(α) = 2 log_q |ια| is the ι-weight; F is punctually ι-pure of weight β ∈ R if all Frobenius eigenvalues have ι-weight β; α is pure of weight n iff ια has absolute value q^{n/2} for every ι, and then α is automatically algebraic.

Hypotheses

  • X of finite type over Z (mixed characteristic allowed); Q̄_ℓ-sheaves with ℓ invertible
  • Weights in (1.2.2) are integers; ι-weights (1.2.6) are real

Deligne weights, purity and the Weil bounds, Part II: Arithmetic cohomology and eigenform applications

Étale cohomology · 1 definition

R34.1Frobenius, algebraicity and weights

Pure numbers, punctually pure and mixed sheaves, ι-weights, twists and real sheavesdefinition

(1.2.1) For q a prime power and n ∈ Z, a number α ∈ Q̄_ℓ is pure of weight n relative to q if it is algebraic and all its complex conjugates have absolute value q^{n/2}. (1.2.2) For X of finite type over Z and a sheaf F on X: F is punctually pure of weight n if for every closed point x the eigenvalues of F_x are pure of weight n relative to N(x); F is mixed if it has a finite filtration with punctually pure successive quotients, whose weights (for nonzero quotients) are the punctual weights of F. The zero sheaf is pure of every weight and mixed with empty weight set. (1.2.3-1.2.4) The same terminology applies to ℓ-adic representations of Gal(k̄/k) for k finite and to Weil sheaves. (1.2.5) Punctually pure sheaves of weight n are stable under subobjects, quotients, extensions, inverse images and finite direct images; tensor products add weights; the dual of a lisse punctually pure sheaf of weight n has weight −n; mixed sheaves are stable under the same operations and tensor products; Q_ℓ(1) is punctually pure of weight −2. (1.2.6) For an isomorphism ι: Q̄_ℓ ≅ C, w_q^ι(α) := 2 log_q |ια| is the ι-weight; punctually ι-pure of weight β ∈ R and ι-mixed are defined accordingly and every representation of W(k̄/k) is automatically ι-mixed. (1.2.7) Twisting by the rank-one Weil sheaf Q_ℓ^{(b)} on Spec F_p (F acting by b ∈ Q̄_ℓ^×) shifts ι-weights by w_p^ι(b). (1.2.12-1.2.14) A lisse F is totally real (resp. ι-real) if the characteristic polynomials of all F_x have totally real algebraic (resp. ι-real) coefficients; a lisse punctually pure F of weight n is a direct summand of the totally real F ⊕ F^∨(−n).

Hypotheses

  • Weights of pure and mixed sheaves are integers by definition; ι-weights may be arbitrary real numbers (Remark 1.2.8), and Theorem 3.4.1 shows a posteriori that for X of finite type over F_p every ι-mixed sheaf is a sum of twists of ι-mixed sheaves with integral weights.
  • (1.2.6): purity of α for every ι implies algebraicity of α; arguments in Weil II treat each ι separately, and Remark 1.2.11 notes that only complex embeddings of the algebraic numbers in Q̄_ℓ are really needed.
  • Conjectures 1.2.9-1.2.10 (every sheaf is ι-mixed; properties of irreducible lisse sheaves with finite-order determinant) are stated, not proved, in the source.

De Rham cohomology from polynomial resolutionsconstruction

For a ring map A→B (or a map of simplicial commutative rings) define dR_(B/A)=|Ω*_(P•/A)|∈D(Mod_A), the direct-sum totalization along antidiagonals of the simplicial cochain complex n↦Ω*_(P_n/A), where P•→B is the canonical free A-algebra resolution. It carries an E∞-algebra structure and a decreasing, separated, exhaustive, multiplicative Hodge filtration Fil_H. The source asserts ('One can show', p.5, line 248, citing [Ill72, §VIII.2.1.1]) that any free resolution may be used, hence dR_(−/A) commutes with filtered colimits; that assertion is not proved in the inspected range. This node does not identify dR_(B/A) with the ordinary de Rham complex of every smooth algebra: see the characteristic-zero-completion-boundary node.

Euler systems and the unconditional cyclotomic main conjecture

Iwasawa theory and special values · 2 constructions

L0Euler systems and their normalization

The cyclotomic-unit Euler system for Z_p(1)construction

Take K = Q. Kummer theory identifies H^1(F,Z_p(1)) with the p-adic completion (F^x)^hat for every extension F of Q. Fix a compatible system {zeta_m} of primitive m-th roots of unity with zeta_{mn}^n = zeta_m. Define c-tilde_{m,infinity} = N_{Q(mu_{mp})/Q(mu_m)}(zeta_{mp} - 1), an element of Q(mu_m)^x inside H^1(Q(mu_m),Z_p(1)), and c-tilde_m = N_{Q(mu_m)/Q(mu_m)^+}(c-tilde_{m,infinity}). Then {c-tilde_{m,infinity}, c-tilde_m} is an Euler system for (Z_p(1), Q^ab, p): the required norm relation is the classical distribution relation N_{Q(mu_{m ell})/Q(mu_m)}(zeta_{m ell} - 1) = (zeta_m - 1) if ell divides m, = (zeta_m - 1)^{1 - Fr_ell^{-1}} if ell does not divide m and m > 1, and = (-1)^{ell-1} ell if m = 1; and the Euler polynomial is det(1 - Fr_ell^{-1} x | Z_p(1)^*) = det(1 - Fr_ell^{-1} x | Z_p) = 1 - x for every prime ell not equal to p.

Hypotheses

  • the compatible system {zeta_m} must satisfy zeta_{mn}^n = zeta_m (Rubin fixes such a collection before (2)); with a non-compatible choice the norm in (2) lands on a Galois conjugate of zeta_m - 1, so the norm compatibilities fail as written (packet-authored remark)
  • the m = 1 case of the distribution relation is genuinely different (it produces (-1)^{ell-1} ell, not a unit), so that conductor must be treated separately
  • the extra norm N_{Q(mu_{mp})/Q(mu_m)} in the definition of c-tilde_{m,infinity} is imposed precisely so that the collection satisfies N_{Q(mu_{mp})/Q(mu_m)} c-tilde_{mp} = c-tilde_m, i.e. so that it is an Euler system in Rubin's sense; Rubin records that this LOSES information
  • these are genuine global units or p-units of Q(mu_m) and of its real subfield: zeta_{mp} - 1 is not a root of unity, in contrast with the ratio (zeta^{-1} - 1)/(zeta - 1) = -zeta^{-1}, which is torsion and carries no arithmetic

Twisting to the chi-component and the unit-to-cohomology dictionaryconstruction

Fix a character chi : G_Q -> O^x of finite order prime to p, assumed EVEN and NONTRIVIAL, with conductor f and fixed field L; put Delta = Gal(L/Q), Q_n the degree-p^n subextension of Q_infinity inside Q(mu_{p^{n+1}}), and L_n = L Q_n. Let T = O_chi, so T^* = Z_p(1) tensor chi^{-1}. Since [L:Q] is prime to p, L intersect Q_n = Q and Delta = Gal(L_n/Q_n) for all n, and restriction gives an isomorphism H^1(Q_n,T^*) = H^1(L_n,T^*)^Delta = (L_n^x tensor-hat O_{chi^{-1}})^Delta = (L_n^x)^chi inside L_n^x tensor-hat O. Twisting the Euler system c-tilde by chi^{-1} (Rubin Prop. II.4.2) gives an Euler system c = c-tilde^{chi^{-1}} for (T^*, Q^ab, p f), whose class c_Q corresponds under the above isomorphism to the product over delta in Gal(Q(mu_f)^+/Q) of (delta c-tilde_f)^{chi^{-1}(delta)}, equivalently the product over delta in Gal(Q(mu_{fp})/Q) of (zeta_{fp}^delta - 1)^{chi^{-1}(delta)}. The chi-cyclotomic units C_{n,chi} are the O[Gal(L_n/Q)]-submodule of E_n^chi generated by xi_{n,chi} (Def. 2.2: for n = 0 the product over Gal(Q(mu_f)/Q) of (zeta_f^delta - 1)^{chi^{-1}(delta)}, for n > 0 the product over Gal(Q_n(mu_{f p^{n+1}})/Q_n) of (zeta_{f p^{n+1}}^delta - 1)^{chi^{-1}(delta)}); at n = 0 this generator is NOT the displayed image of c_Q, which by (6) equals xi_{L,chi}^{1 - chi^{-1}(p)}.

Hypotheses

  • chi is even, nontrivial, of finite order PRIME TO p; the prime-to-p order is what makes the chi-component a direct summand and makes L intersect Q_n = Q
  • chi is viewed as a Dirichlet character modulo f, with the convention chi(q) = 0 when q divides f and chi(q) = chi(Fr_q) otherwise; this convention matters in the formula c_Q = xi_{L,chi}^{1 - chi^{-1}(p)}
  • the identification of H^1(Q_n,T^*) with (L_n^x)^chi is by restriction followed by the completed tensor product; it identifies the FULL H^1, not a Selmer subgroup
  • the definition of xi_{n,chi} differs between n = 0 (product over Gal(Q(mu_f)/Q) of (zeta_f^delta - 1)^{chi^{-1}(delta)}) and n > 0 (product over Gal(Q_n(mu_{f p^{n+1}})/Q_n) of (zeta_{f p^{n+1}}^delta - 1)^{chi^{-1}(delta)})

Faltings finiteness, semisimplicity and isogeny theorems

Curves, abelian varieties and Shimura varieties · 2 definitions · 3 constructions

R28.1Height finiteness on arithmetic moduli

Semiabelian schemes and the Hodge line bundle omega_{A/S}definition

For a scheme (or algebraic stack) S, a semiabelian variety of relative dimension g over S is a smooth algebraic group p : G -> S whose fibres are connected of dimension g and are extensions of an abelian variety by a torus. With s : S -> A the zero section one sets omega_{A/S} = s^*(Omega^g_{A/S}), a line bundle on S. It satisfies: (a) omega_{A/S} = p_*(Omega^g_{A/S}) when p is proper; (b) it commutes with base change; (c) if A = Pic^tau(C/S) for a stable curve q : C -> S then omega_{A/S} = Lambda^g q_*(omega_{C/S}) with omega_{C/S} the relative dualizing module; (d) for S = Spec(C) and p proper, omega_{A/S} = Gamma(A, Omega^g_{A/C}) carries the canonical hermitian product <alpha,beta> = (i/2)^g int_A alpha ^ conj(beta).

Hypotheses

  • S a scheme or algebraic stack; p : G -> S smooth with connected fibres of dimension g, each fibre an extension of an abelian variety by a torus
  • for (a): p proper (i.e. A/S abelian scheme)
  • for (c): q : C -> S a stable curve of genus g in the sense of Deligne-Mumford, and A = Pic^tau(C/S)
  • for (d): S = Spec(C) and p proper, so that A/C is a complex abelian variety

FaltingsFinitenessAndIsogenyTheorems:R28.1/semiabelian-scheme-and-its-hodge-line-bundle

Metrized line bundles on Spec(R), their degree, and the modular height h(A)definition

For K a number field with ring of integers R, a metrized line bundle on Spec(R) is a projective R-module P of rank 1 together with norms ||.||_v on P otimes_R K_v for every infinite place v of K; put e_v = 1 if K_v = R and e_v = 2 if K_v = C. Its degree is Grad(P, ||.||) = log(#(P/R.p)) - sum_v e_v log ||p||_v for any nonzero p in P (independent of p by the product formula). For p : A -> Spec(R) semiabelian with proper generic fibre A/K, omega_{A/R} is metrized at the infinite places by ||alpha||_v^2 = (i/2)^g int_{A(K_v)} alpha ^ conj(alpha), and the modular height is h(A) = Grad(omega_{A/R}) / [K : Q]. It is invariant under extension of the ground field.

Hypotheses

  • K a number field, R = O_K
  • p : A -> Spec(R) semiabelian with proper generic fibre A/K (properness of the generic fibre is what makes the archimedean Hodge product defined)
  • the archimedean metric is the canonical Hodge product of node semiabelian-scheme-and-its-hodge-line-bundle (d)
  • no polarization is required for the definition of h(A)

A proper stack over Spec(Z) carrying a stable curve dominating principally polarized moduliconstruction

There exists over Spec(Z) a proper algebraic stack J, an open substack U subset J and a proper morphism psi : U -> A_g (the stack of principally polarized abelian varieties of relative dimension g) extending to psibar : J/Q -> Abar_g/Q, such that over J the following exist: (a) a stable curve q : C -> J; (b) a sub-line-bundle (locally a direct summand) L subset Lambda^g q_*(omega_{C/Z}); (c) over U a pair of group homomorphisms alpha : Pic^tau(C/J) -> psi^*(A) and beta : psi^*(A) -> Pic^tau(C/J) with alpha o beta = multiplication by some d in N, d != 0 (A the universal abelian variety over A_g); (d) over J tensor_Z Q an isomorphism L^{otimes r} = psibar^*(M), with L over U/Q the image of alpha^* : psi^*(omega_{A/A_g}) -> Lambda^g q_*(omega_{C/Z}), and the resulting isomorphism psi^*(omega_{A/A_g})^{otimes r} = psi^*(M) over U/Q is the psi^*-pullback of the isomorphism used in the construction of M over A_g.

Hypotheses

  • g fixed; A_g the algebraic stack of principally polarized abelian varieties of relative dimension g, A_g its coarse moduli space, Mbar_g the proper Deligne-Mumford stack of stable curves of genus gtilde
  • r > 0 such that (omega_{A/A_g})^{otimes r} is very ample on A_g/Q (Baily-Borel), Abar_g/Q the Zariski closure of A_g/Q in the corresponding P^N_Q, Abar_g/Z its closure in P^N_Z, and M = O(1) on Abar_g/Z
  • over C a proper dominant morphism phi : N -> Abar_g/C over which the universal abelian variety extends to a semiabelian variety with omega^{otimes r} = phi^*(M) (Namikawa's toroidal compactification)
